Definition: An Among-among is Tengger's protection rite for 44-day-old babies. The term derives from the word among (“to care for, to nurture”), and in reduplicated form refers to a special slametan or feast to show gratitude for children. The ritual includes the recitation of protective mantras at each stage of the baby’s development, along with prohibitions imposed on the mother, such as avoidance of consuming sea fish, spicy food, and cucumbers and recommendation of consuming ranti,sawijo, and tetirem leaves. After 44 days, the prohibitions are lifted and household life returns to normal.
Etymology: among (amOG) : I 1 kw. momong; 2 (-gêni) êngg. tunggu gêni (ingarêp kêrên lsp); kaki (nini) [x]: lêlêmbut kang ngêmong bayi (wong); di-[x]-i êngg: disugoni (tmr.gêni). II [x]-[x] êngg: bancakan (slamêtan tmr. bocah). III êngg: 1 mung; 2 nanging.
Variants:
selapanan
slametan bayi
mitoni cilik
bancakan anak
Examples: The Tengger people observe the Among-among tradition when an infant turns 44 days old as a rite of protection and gratitude for the child's healthy growth.
Reference:
- Sukmawan, S., Al Fathi, R. L., Salamah, Satwika, P. W., Salma, W., & Sutopo, F. Z. S. (2023). Buku saku budaya dan bahasa Jawa dialek Tengger. Inoffast Publishing.
- Proyek Sasana Budaya. (1978). Upacara Kasada dan beberapa adat istiadat masyarakat Tengger. Direktorat Jenderal Kebudayaan, Departemen Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan.
- Sutarto, A. (2006). Sekilas tentang masyarakat Tengger. Badan Pembinaan Hukum Nasional. bphn.go.id

Definition: A square-shaped offering container made of woven bamboo, used in customary ceremonies to serve ritual offerings. In Tengger wedding ceremonies, it is used to present fermented cassava, pipis, jajadah, bananas, areca nuts, and betel leaves as a symbol of openness and receptivity to blessings.
Etymology: ancak : KN. platte vierkante schotel of hordetje van gevlochten bamboe (met pisangbladen er op als schotel gebruikt bij feestelijke gelegenheden waarop gekookte rijst met de noodige toespijzen den gasten voorgediend wordt, die dan met hun vieren of vijven daarvan eten, vrg. kêmarang, ambêng, Wk.). Ook om bv. offerspijzen op te leggen (of iets, zooals visch, op te droogen of te rooken JR.) Bab. Mat. I, 17 (vrg. èncèk JZ. II) Bab. Jo. II, 286. kaungkulan ancak, sarta dipun sawiyah, een vernederende behandeling ondergaan. ° kodhok een soort ancak Tj. I, 588. ancak agra, eign, van een Butå G. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: Various traditional snacks and offerings were neatly arranged on the ancak for the wedding ceremony.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tenggerese en de Tenggeroezen. Weltevreden.

Definition: A Barikan is Tengger's protection rite. Grounded in the belief in the relationship between humans, nature, ancestors, and supernatural forces, the rite serves to restore disrupted harmony. Barikan is held at customary leader's residence and led by the village dukun (shaman). The food offerings in this rite are split to two: one portion to be consumed together during the ritual gathering, and another taken home as offerings in yards and fields. Beyond spiritual protection, barikan is also understood as an expression of gratitude and social solidarity strengthening.
Etymology: barik : KN. 1. = dharik, of larik, niet in Wk. — 2. barikan, tijdelijk heerschend gebruik, eig. regel? vgl. parikan. uit bijgeloovigheid, bv. een ring van klapperdop aan den vinger dragen, als behoedmiddel tegen een heerschende ziekte, de een of andere kost als offerande aan de booze geesten geven met hetzelfde doel; ook een tijdelijk heerschende modegril Wk. saiki ° wong ikêt-ikêtan dipun cundhuki wulu blêkok, nu heerscht de mode om een pluimpje van blěkok-vederen op den hoofddoek te dragen Wk. — borak-barik, zie ald. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918. barik : KN. 1. = dharik, atau larch, tidak ada di Wk. - 2. barikan, kebiasaan yang berlaku sementara, bdk. parikan. karena takhayul, misal: memakai cincin genta di jari, sebagai pelindung dari penyakit yang sedang mewabah, memberikan makanan sebagai persembahan kepada roh jahat dengan maksud yang sama; juga merupakan kebiasaan yang berlaku sementara di Wk. saiki ° wong ikêt-ikêtan dipun cundhuki wulu blêkok, sekarang sudah menjadi mode memakai bulu blěkok di kerudung Wk. - borak-barik, lihat di sana. Sumber: Kamus Tangan Jawa-Belanda, Gericke dan Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: During the Barikan ritual, women bring baskets of cooked food to be blessed by the village priest, after which half is shared among the community and the rest is taken home as a protective blessing.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1927). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. Djawa: Tijdschrift van het Java-Instituut, 7, 23–37, 217–31, 291–304.

- Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Dimensi ekologi folklor Unan-Unan Tengger. Jurnal Ilmiah Edukasi & Sosial, 11(1), 60–66.

Definition: A guardian spirit believed to inhabit specific places such as houses, trees, or natural sites in the belief system of the Tengger community. As a supernatural entity, it maintains balance between the human world and spirit realm and is invoked in rituals by traditional leaders. Often regarded as an ancestor, danyang, or pepunden, it safeguards the physical and spiritual life of the community.
Etymology: baurêksa : 1 ghost or spirit that inhabits a certain place. 2 one who has long held sway in a certain place. sing m-[x] guardian spirit of a house, tree, etc. Sumber: Javanese-English Dictionary, Horne, 1974, #1968.
Examples: The Tengger community seeks protection from the bau rekso, who is believed to be the guardian spirit of the area.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger Tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Sukmawan, S., & Febriani, R. (2018). Perempuan-perempuan pemeluk erat adat: Studi etnografi perempuan Tengger. Linguista: Jurnal Ilmiah Bahasa, Sastra, dan Pembelajarannya, 2(1), 1–10.

Definition: A bowl-shaped container made of metal, used to carry water, flowers, or ritual offerings during customary ceremonies. It features a supporting stand at the bottom and serves as a symbolic medium of presentation. In wedding customs, it functions as a medium of exchange containing betel leaves and tobacco during the asrah pengantèn procession.
Etymology: bokor : KN. metalen kom met een rand van onder als voetstuk BTDj. 12, (vrg. cêmung). Vlg. ZG. XVIII, 139 ter reiniging der vingers vóor en na het eten. pangombèn nèng °, BG. 250. gêlung bokor mêngkurêp = ° bokoran, zie ben. Vlg. anderen heet dit gêlung bukur kumurêp, Wk., van bukur, I. waluh bokor, zie waluh. jêruk bokor, een soort jěruk met zeer losse schil Rh. — bokoran, op de wijze van een bòkòr: en bijzondere wijze van opmaken van het haar, gebruikelijk als bruidskapsel. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: The bride handed a bokor containing betel leaves and tobacco to the groom during the asrah pengantèn procession.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tenggerese en de Tenggeroezen. Weltevreden.

Definition: A traditional body scrub or ointment consisting of fragrant flowers, spices, and censecrated water, used in bodily purification rites during customary ceremonies. It is rubbed on the shoulders, neck, and feet of the bride and groom as a symbol of physical and spiritual cleansing before entering a new phase of life. Beyond its use as a fragrance, it serves as a medium for channeling prayers and blessings.
Etymology: borèh : N. konyoh, K. een uit kruiden en bloemen gemaakt welriekend smeersel, zalf, blanketsel; het gele van atal bereide smeersel, waarmee bruid en bruigom en anderen bij plechtige gelegenheden bestreken worden PL. I, 155; II, 161. ° wangi, een bruine, sterk geparfumeerde soort boreh. kêmbang borèh, welriekende bloemen ZG. XIV, 250, ook wel bloemen tot borèh, gebruikt ib. XXI, 125. — baborèh, zich met borèh, insmeeren L. 192. — amborèhi, ngonyohi, met borèh bestrijken, besmeren. — borehan, met borèh besmeerd Waj. I, 37. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: The shaman applied borèh to the neck and shoulders of the bride and groom as a symbol of physical and spiritual purification.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: A traditional riddle based on wordplay and poetic allegories, performed in Tengger Karo rituals after the main prayer. Consisting of wangsalan, it is delivered sequentially by the shaman to serve as sacred entertainment and convey symbolic wisdom.
Etymology: cangkriman : KN. raadsel; en een raadsel of (ook elkander) raadsels opgeven. — nyangkrimani, iemand een raadsel opgeven. — cêcangkriman, L. 226: mekaar raadsels opgeven. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: The wordplay embedded in cangkriman serves not only as a witty riddle, but also conveys profound symbolic wisdom.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Sodoran-Karo: Telaga edukasi, seni, tradisi, dan gastronomi Tengger. MNC Publishing.

Definition: The first ancestor who opened, established, and sustained a territory or community, particularly a village honored as the spiritual founder and original protector. In Tengger tradition, it is not only regarded as a physical pioneer but also as a sacred figure who dedicated their life to collective well-being. The ancestor's name is continually invoked in communal prayers, and their grave becomes a center of pilgrimage and intergenerational reverence.
Etymology: cakal bakal (cakal bakal) : K.N. de eerste ontginner van een grond; de eerste aanlegger of stichter van een dorp op plaats; de voorouders [vrg. akal bakal]. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16.
Examples: The Tengger community continuously offers prayers for the cikal bakal, who cleared the land and established their village.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., & Febriani, R. (2018). Perempuan-perempuan pemeluk erat adat: Studi etnografi perempuan Tengger. Linguista: Jurnal Ilmiah Bahasa, Sastra, dan Pembelajarannya, 2(1), 1–10.

Definition: A guardian spirit of a particular region or place in the belief system of the Tengger community that is not always associated with human souls. Serving as a supernatural protector, it maintains harmony beween nature, humans, and the spirit world. It is often positioned on the same level as baureksa, pepunden, or ancestors, safeguarding the physical and spiritual life of the community.
Etymology: dhanyang (Da¥aG) : kn 1 ([x] baurêksa, [x] pakayangan) dhêmit sing mbaurêksa ing sawijining panggonan; 2 ak. sanggan ut. congkok tembok; kc. bau-dhanyang, dhanghyang. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: The Tengger community presents offerings to honor the danyang, who is believed to guard the peace of the village.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., & Febriani, R. (2018). Perempuan-perempuan pemeluk erat adat: Studi etnografi perempuan Tengger. Linguista: Jurnal Ilmiah Bahasa, Sastra, dan Pembelajarannya, 2(1), 1–10.

Definition: The Entas-entas ritual purifies ancestors. More than a mere act of reverence, this ceremony is collective in nature and is performed once the family is economically and socially sufficient. It represents the spiritual bond between the family and their ancestors through a series of complex sacred rites, large-scale offerings, and the symbolic representation of the spirit in the form of pètro made from young coconut leaves and leaves.
Etymology: êntas (|ntas) : êngg mêntas bae; di-[x](-i) kn: 1 dijupuk saka ing (banyu, anglo, pamemean lsp); 2 dipitulungi (saka rêribêd, bêbaya); 3 ak. diomah-omahake; di-[x]-i ak: dirampungake (tmr. pagawean); di-[x]-ake: 1 ditulungi supaya mêntas, digawa mêntas; 2 ak. diomah-omahake; 3 dipitulungi (saka ing rêribêd, bêbaya); kc. mêntas, pêntasan. Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Variants:
mentas
mentas saka kolam
mentas adus
nyewu
Examples: The Tenggerese family holds the Entas-entas ceremony as a sacred post-mortem rite to purify their ancestors' spirits and ensure their passage to heaven.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Bahar, Z. R., & Sukmawan, S. (2021). Bethek-sinoman: Memupuk gotong royong, menopang anjangsana, dan memelihara jati diri masyarakat Tengger. Sosioglobal: Jurnal Pemikiran dan Penelitian Sosiologi, 6(1), 11–26. 
- Sutarto, A. (2006). Sekilas tentang masyarakat Tengger. Balai Kajian Sejarah dan Nilai Tradisional Yogyakarta.

Definition: A symbolic representation of the prospective bride used in Tengger engagement riddles. Used during customary cangkriman riddles, it symbolizes the cow representing the bride to be exchanged for rambon (the groom) through metaphorical dialogue between representatives of both families.
Etymology:
jawi (jawi) : I. K.N. een wilde koe, het wijfje van den wilden stier: ook jêjawi [Ml. koe]. II. K. zie jawa en jaba.
Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16. jawi (jawi) : I k jaba. II k: jawa. III (ut. jêjawi) kn: banthèng, sapi alasan.
Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: In the engagement riddle dialogue of the Tengger tradition, the bride's family uses the term jawi to symbolically represent the prospective bride.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A scared talisman consisting of old garments and ancient coins,  kept in a sanctified repository and used by the village chief shaman during important rituals. Used in ceremonies such as Karo, this ancestral object undergoes purification through incense fumigation, placement on banana leaves, and rewrapping before being returned to its repository. It symbolizes spiritual continuity, the legitimacy of the shaman's leadership, and divine protection for the community.
Etymology: jimat : barang ingkang dipun simpên margi dipun arah sawabipun. Sumber: Babasan lan Saloka, Anonim, 1908, #1278. jimat : 1 good luck charm, amulet. 2 var of JIMPIT. Sumber: Javanese-English Dictionary, Horne, 1974, #1968.
Examples: Consisting of ancient garments and coins, the jimat klontongan serves as a sacred ancestral talisman that symbolizes divine protection for the community.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Sodoran as a means of intromission education for Tenggerese younger generation. In Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Local Wisdom, ICLW 2020, 25 November 2020, Jakarta, Indonesia.

Definition: An annual customary ceremony held by the Tengger community as an expression of gratitude to Sang Hyang Widi for agricultural harvests and a form of reverence to ancestors and village guardian spirits. The ritual is marked by offerings of agricultural produce and sacred food placed at temples, mountains, or other sacred sites, alongside the recitation of mantras, artistic performances, and communal feasts. This ceremony fosters communal solidarity, strengthens cultural identity, and reflects a cosmological balance among humans, nature, and the supernatural.
Etymology:
Sedekah Karo is an annual ceremony of the Tengger people held on the 14th day of the month of Karo in the Tengger calendar. This celebration is held to honor the legendary figures Setija and Toehoe, as well as to pray for the safety of the entire village (Jasper, 1927: 47).
The ceremony includes communal prayers, the presentation of offerings, riddle games (tjangkriman), and dance performances such as tajoeŋan or sodorran. According to Hefner (1989: 114), Sedekah Karo reflects the harmony between ancient Hindu-Javanese traditions and local Islamic influences in the spiritual life of the Tengger community. “Karo is the name of the second month in the Tengger calendar. During this month, the Tengger people hold ceremonies, commemorative events, and celebrations to honor, remember, and seek blessings from the spirits and the souls of those who have passed away” (Sukmawan, 2018:76)
Variants:
Hari Raya Karo
Upacara Karo
Sedekah Karo
Yadnya Karo
Karoan
Examples: The Tenggerese people celebrate the annual Karo ceremony as a sacred expression of gratitude for agricultural harvests and a tribute to their ancestors.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1927). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. Djawa: Tijdschrift van het Java-Instituut.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: The first month in the Tengger ritual calendar, occurring around late June to early July. It is marked by leg shadows pointing south and natural signs in the betik freshwater fish, signaling the beginning of the planting season and the agricultural-spiritual cycle.
Etymology: kasa (kOsO) : kn. mangsa kang kapisan (22 Juni - 2 Agustus). Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: The Tengger community begins their ritual calendar and planting season in the month of kasa.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggerreezen. Weltevreden: G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A month and major ritual cycle in Tengger culture, culminating in offerings made at the crater of Mount Bromo.
Examples: The Kasada ritual is held in the twelfth month of the Tengger calendar.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sutarto, A. (2006). Sekilas tentang masyarakat Tengger. Balai Kajian Sejarah dan Nilai Tradisional Yogyakarta.

Definition: A ritual figure in cangkriman performed in Karo rituals who answers riddles posed by Ardijaya. Performed by assistants of the shaman such as legen, sepuh, or sanggar, this character represents collective reasoning and also appears in Sodoran Dance.
Etymology:
Kertidjaja adalah anggota dewan tjangkriman yang bertugas menjawab teka-teki atau pertanyaan yang dilemparkan oleh Bolèngan, serta mewakili nalar kolektif dalam struktur permainan ritual. Nama ini berasal dari akar kata kerthi (mulia, bijak) dan jaya (menang, unggul), menunjukkan peran simboliknya sebagai penjaga logika dan pemecah makna. Ia bisa dianggap sebagai semacam pujangga desa dadakan dalam konteks upacara. Jika gagal menjawab, ia bisa dihukum dengan minum sadjeng (Jasper, 1928: 50). "Cangkriman Kertijoyo lazimnya dibawakan (dibacakan) oleh dukun pandita berdampingan dengan salah-satu pembantu dukun. Dinamai Cangkriman Kertijoyo karena nama salah satu karakter penampilnya adalah Kertijoyo. Karakter/tokoh Kertijoyo diperankan oleh salah satu asisten dukun (legen, sepuh, atau sanggar). Sementara itu, dukun pandita memerankan tokoh Ardijoyo. Ardijoyo bertindak sebagai ‘pelempar’
teka-teki, Kertijoyo bertindak sebagai penjawab teka-teki. Cangkriman Kertijoyo mengiringi atau tepatnya mengawali pementasan tari Sodoran pada perayaan Hari Raya Karo." (Sukmawan, 2018: 126).
Examples: The character Kertijaya represents the collective reasoning of the Tenggerese community at the beginning of the Sodoran Dance performance.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: A spiritual assistant figure who accompanies or substitutes the chief shaman in minor ceremonies. His duties include leading prayers, sprinkling holy water, and ringing ritual bells during ceremonies when the main shaman is unable to attend.
Etymology: Legèn adalah asisten atau wakil dari dukun utama dalam masyarakat Tengger yang memiliki wewenang terbatas untuk memimpin upacara kecil, terutama ketika dukun sedang menjalani puasa moetih atau tidak bisa hadir. Dalam beberapa upacara seperti sedekah Kasangga, legèn memimpin pawai keliling desa, menyebarkan air suci dan membacakan doa sambil diiringi bunyi lonceng ritual. Secara struktur, legèn berada di bawah doekoen tjilik dan berperan sebagai pelaksana teknis dalam kegiatan spiritual (Jasper, 1928: 53). "Legen adalah pembantu dukun Tengger yang bertugas mempersiapkan keperluan atau sajian yang terkait dengan kegiatan upacara. Mbok Legen adalah istri Legen yang secara faktual lebih banyak berperan dalam penyiapan sesaji." (Sukmawan, 2018:68). “...waarbij worden gevoegd: twee kleine boemboengs of kokers met legèn (palmwijn)…”(Jasper, 1928, hlm. 73)
Examples: A legèn accompanies the chief shaman by ringing ritual bells throughout the ceremonial procession.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: Mandi is a woven bamboo basket used as a container for offerings, sacrifices, or gifts in traditional ceremonies, particularly in the Tengger wedding procession. In a marriage ceremony, mandi is filled with rice and fruits and presented by the groom’s family to the bride as part of the symbolic dowry.
Etymology: Mandi dalam konteks budaya Tengger bukan berarti "mandi" dalam pengertian umum (membersihkan diri dengan air), melainkan sebuah keranjang anyaman bambu yang berfungsi sebagai wadah sesaji, persembahan, atau hadiah pernikahan. Dalam prosesi pernikahan, mandi diisi dengan beras dan buah-buahan, dan diserahkan oleh mempelai pria kepada pihak mempelai perempuan sebagai pelengkap dari mas kawin (Jasper, 1928: 71).
Examples: The groom's family presents a mandi filled with rice and fruits as an offering container during the Tengger customary wedding procession.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A cleansing ritual held by the village community to repel misfortunes and maintain cosmic balance. Performed collectively, this tradition purifies the living space from evil spirits and negative energies while nurturing harmony between humans, ancestors, and nature.
Etymology: "mayu (mayu) : I êngg. kn. masang payoning omah; kc. payu. II ut. mêmayu kw. agawe bêcik, mbêbêcik; kc. ayu, hayu. Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75. desa (desO) : 1 (S) kw. ak. panggonan, keblat; 2 n. dhusun k. gêgrombolaning pomahan ing sajabaning nêgara (luwih gêdhe tinimbang dhukuh); njajah [x] milang kori pr: njajah mênyang ngêndi-êndi; [x] mawa cara, nêgara mawa tata pr: ing sabên panggonan duwe padatan (tata-cara) dhewe-dhewe; ndesani: kaku, ora luwês; padesan; kaklumpukane desa-desa, wêwêngkoning desa. Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: Held after the inauguration of a new village chief, the Mayu desa ceremony serves to spiritually purify the village and invite blessings for the community.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Sodoran-Karo: Telaga edukasi, seni, tradisi, dan gastronomi Tengger. MNC Publishing.

Definition: A symbolic wedding ritual performed in Tengger where the groom makes the first stab at the nape of a sacrificial animal. The ceremony marks the beginning of animal slaughter, usually a cow or buffalo, as an offering to Batarakala to ward off evil and protect the village. In some cases, a white buffalo is sacrificed to invoke safety for the entire community.
Etymology: Medoedoek adalah tindakan simbolik berupa tusukan pertama oleh mempelai pria terhadap hewan kurban (biasanya lembu atau sapi) sebagai bagian dari pelaksanaan nazar (nadar) dalam rangkaian upacara pernikahan adat Tengger. Tusukan ini dilakukan pada bagian belakang leher hewan, sebelum disembelih (Jasper, 1928: 74–75). "Ritual Mbeduduk, yakni adanya sebuah penyembelihan hewan kerbau yang dipersembahkan kepada Batarakala. Batarakala diundang untuk makan-makan, lalu diminta untuk melakukan sebuah perjanjian agar setelah diberikan sesaji-sesaji tersebut, para Batarakala pergi menjauh dari desa tersebut, dan tidak menganggu masyarakat dan lingkungannya. Dalam ritual ini, kerbau yang disajikan adalah kerbau yang spesial, yaitu seekor kerbau putih yang disembelih, dan dipersembahkan secara khusus kepada para Batarakala." (Sukmawan, 2018: 21).
Examples: The groom performs meduduk by stabbing the sacrificial animal's nape as part of a vow and offering for safety in a Tengger traditional wedding.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: A animal sacrifice procession performed in Tengger to fulfill a sacred vow. The process consists of tying the animal days before the event, prayers led by a ritual specialist, circling the animal three times for purification, and concluding with meduduk performed by the groom.
Etymology: Mekakat adalah keseluruhan prosesi pengurbanan hewan dalam rangka menepati janji suci (nadar), yang mencakup pengikatan hewan beberapa hari sebelum upacara, pembacaan doa oleh dukun, perputaran mengelilingi hewan sebanyak tiga kali, dan diakhiri dengan tindakan medoedoek (Jasper, 1928: 75).
Examples: The Tengger community performs the mekakat procession as a fulfillment of a sacred vow and animal purification during traditional ceremonies.
Reference: Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A traditional bamboo shoulder pole used by the Tengger people to transport ritual offerings, especially during the Kasada ceremony. Etymologically, the name derives from the Javanese word ongkèk, meaning a two-sided shoulder pole. In practice, it carries agricultural produce, flowers, and livestock to sacred sites such as the crater of Mount Bromo, serving as a medium that connects humans, nature, and ancestors. Beyond its practical function, the pole has expanded to become a symbol of offering itself.
Etymology: ongkèk (oGkE?) : I kn pikulan ing kiwa têngên nganggo sikilan ut. ambèn-ambènan (dianggo mikul gamêlan lsp). II di-[x]-[x] êngg. kn: diogak-ogak supaya rubuh. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: Each family decorates an ongkek using bamboo, young coconut leaves, and agricultural produce as a sacred symbol of devotion to the ancestors.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Proyek Sasana Budaya. (1978). Upacara Kasada dan beberapa adat istiadat masyarakat Tengger. Direktorat Jenderal Kebudayaan, Departemen Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan.
-   Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Sodoran-Karo: Telaga edukasi, seni, tradisi, dan gastronomi Tengger. MNC Publishing.

Definition: A sacred ritual garment worn by Tengger ritual leaders during religious ceremonies. The attire is a knee-length, unstitched robe made from triangular cotton fabrics in colorful, slanted patchwork patterns resembling batik. In local belief, it is believed to merge with the wearer's body and is endowed with supernatural potency, serving as a sacred heirloom that connects humans with the ancestral realm.
Etymology: Ook n. v. e. ander buis BTDj. 49; en in Těnggěr n. v. het kleed door de priesters gedragen ZG. XXIX, bl. 371. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918. Binêktanan rasukan Ăntakusuma, tuwin caping basunănda, punapadene tarumpah padakacarma, sinungakên ing Sang Parta, W.W. 68-9 dadi anan(...) mbi Ăntakusuma ora dhèk jaman kuwalèn, kaya kang kêsêbut ing layang babad, wis dhèk jaman kadewatan. ăntakusuma (OntOkusumO) : Binêktanan rasukan Ăntakusuma, tuwin caping basunănda, punapadene tarumpah padakacarma, sinungakên ing Sang Parta, W.W. 68-9 dadi anan(...) mbi Ăntakusuma ora dhèk jaman kuwalèn, kaya kang kêsêbut ing layang babad, wis dhèk jaman kadewatan. Sumber: Têmbung Bêcik, Padmasusastra, 1898, #13.
Examples: The ritual leader wears the sacred ontokusumo robe during religious ceremonies to connect the community with the ancestral realm.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Setiawati, E., Rizal, M. S., & Febriani, R. (2020). Sodoran as a means of intromission education for Tenggerese younger generation. In Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Local Wisdom, ICLW 2020, 25 November 2020, Jakarta, Indonesia.

Definition: An offering container made of banana leaves in the shape of a small house, used in Tengger rituals to hold traditional cakes for ancestors and spirits. Consisting of traditional delicacies such as apem and djoewadah, it also refers to a cone-shaped rice flour cake that symbolizes a person's spiritual readiness to face death.
Etymology:
pasung (pasUG) : K.N. naam van een soort van gebak. -masung, Pasoeng bereiden.
Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16.
Examples: Villagers arrange offerings in a banana-leaf pasung container to be presented to the ancestors during the Karo ceremony.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S. (2022). Buku saku Pujan Kasanga. Universitas Brawijaya.

Definition: A ritual flower effigy made up of coconut leaves and flowers used in Tengger spiritual ceremonies. This object serves as a symbolic medium representing ancestral spirits, village guardian spirits, and the founders of the settlement. It is invoked during various important ceremonies, such as weddings, Entas-entas, and spirit summoning rituals. The making of Petra is the responsibility of wong sepuh (senior residents) who are attendants with spiritual authority within the community. Its presence signifies the connection between the human world and the ancestral realm.
Etymology:
patung-patung bunga (petra) yang akan digunakan untuk memohon arwah leluhur yang telah meninggal. Pembuatan patung-patung petra adalah tanggung jawab wong sepuh, atau “asisten ritual sesepuh” pendeta (Hefner, 1985: 121). 
“petro” atau boneka laki-laki dan perempuan, yang didalamnya terdapat arwah nenek moyang (Jesper, 1927:6). 
Pètro adalah simbol arwah (sosok zielebeeld atau citra roh) yang dibuat untuk mewakili roh-roh leluhur, makhluk halus pelindung desa (baoereksa), dan para pendiri desa (tjakal-bakal). 
Pètro dihadirkan dalam berbagai upacara, termasuk pernikahan dan sedekah entas-entas (1000 hari kematian), sebagai tanda kehadiran simbolik mereka (Jasper, 1928: 73–74). 
"Petra merupakan simbol arwah leluhur. Petra bagian atas (kepala) terbuat dari daun tlotok yang memiliki makna telu tok, yakni lahir, urip, mati." (Sukmawan, 2018:44).
Examples: The Tenggerese community uses the petra—a ritual flower effigy made of coconut leaves—as a symbolic medium representing ancestral spirits during sacred ceremonies.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Jasper, J. E. (1927). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. Djawa: Tijdschrift van het Java-Instituut
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A sacred ceremonial space in the middle of the sand field at Mount Bromo, serving as the main altar during the Kasada ceremony in the Tengger community. At this site, shamans lead prayers and worship directed toward spiritual protectors such as Sunan Pernata, using ritual implements such as prapen (incense holder), prasen (holy water vessel), and offerings. It functions as the center of veneration, spiritual unity, and sacred communication between humans and the divine realm in Tengger religious tradition.
Etymology: Potèn adalah tempat suci di tengah Lautan Pasir Gunung Bromo yang menjadi titik kumpul utama dalam upacara Kasada. Di sinilah para dukun memanjatkan doa bersama kepada Sunan Pernata, pelindung spiritual tempat tersebut, sebelum melanjutkan perjalanan ke kawah. Lokasi ini dikelilingi pagar sederhana dan menjadi semacam sanggar terbuka yang menghadap langsung ke kerucut Bromo (Jasper, 1928: 54). Poten adalah ruang suci berbentuk panggung upacara yang terletak di lautan pasir Gunung Bromo, menjadi pusat penyelenggaraan ritual keagamaan masyarakat Tengger, terutama pada perayaan Kasada. Poten berfungsi sebagai altar terbuka yang dilengkapi dengan perlengkapan ritus seperti prapen (tempat dupa), prasen (bejana tirta), dan berbagai sesaji (Hefner, 1989: 49-50).
Examples: The Tengger community gathers at the poten to perform communal prayers before casting offerings into the crater of Mount Bromo.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger Tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.

Definition: An incense burner used in Javanese customary rituals serving as a medium for prayer, offerings, and spiritual communication. Made of clay or metal, it is placed near the sanggar during ceremonies such as weddings, entas-entas, or village cleansing rites. Its smoke is believed to convey sacred messages to ancestors or the supernatural realm.
Etymology: prapèn (prapEn) : kn. wadhah gêni (luwêng) ing pandhe (kêmasan). Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75. prapèn : fireplace; place for an open fire, e.g. a blacksmith's forge. See also API. Sumber: Javanese-English Dictionary, Horne, 1974, #1968.
Examples: Smoke from the prapèn rose high, accompanying the prayers recited during the entas-entas ceremony.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: A ritual container used for holding tirta or holy water in Tengger customary ceremonies. Used in rituals such as walagara, weddings, and funerary rites, it serves as a medium of purification and a conduit of blessings. The water within it, known as air wasuh padha, is used to wash the feet of ancestors or deities, symbolically purifying humans and bridging the spiritual and physical realms.
Etymology: Prasen adalah wadah khusus untuk menampung tirta atau air suci dalam rangkaian upacara keagamaan di masyarakat Tengger. Dalam slametan walagara, prasen ditempatkan bersama alat upacara lainnya di dekat sesaji, dan digunakan oleh dukun untuk memercikkan air suci sebagai penanda keberkahan dan pensucian (Jasper, 1928: 72). Menurut Sutarto (2006: 10-12), prasen juga digunakan dalam upacara pernikahan dan kematian menjadikannya sebagai benda ritual yang membawa sifat pembersih dan penyambung antara dunia manusia dan dunia roh. "Prasen adalah wadah air suci. Istilah lainnya yang digunakan untuk menyebut prasen adalah siwamba, yakni tempat air wasuh padha. Air wasuh padha adalah air yang dipakai untuk menyucikan kaki para dewa/dewi dan para leluhur. Setelah itu, air tersebut dapat digunakan untuk menyucikan diri sendiri." (Sukmawan, 2018:122).
Examples: The shaman sprinkles holy water from the prasen to purify the community during the walagara ceremony.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sutarto, A. (2006). Sekilas tentang Masyarakat Tengger. Komisi Kebudayaan dan Pariwisata Kabupaten Probolinggo.
- Sukmawan, S. (2018). Perempuan-Perempuan Pemeluk Erat Adat: Studi Etnografi Perempuan Tengger. Universitas Brawijaya.

Definition: A communal worship and prayer ritual within the Tengger village ritual calendar.
Etymology:
Pujan, From the Sanskrit and Old Javanese term for  "worship," Tengger pujan are celebrated in the fourth, eighth, ninth, and twelfth months of the Tengger calendar year; several villages celebrate a fifth pujan in the seventh month, in addition. Once marked by feasting at the village priest's house, pujan today involve a brief invocation and meal at the priest's house. Supported by food contributions from all households in the village, attendance is restricted to village officials and the priest (Hefner, 1989:112-113).  

The pujan illustrates this pattern clearly, and also shows to what degree ordinary villagers are drawn into the ceremony... The actual ritual service—a more or less standard invocation of the gods—lasts only about five minutes. The remainder of the evening is devoted to the meal... The pujan circuit is completed the following morning. Trays of cooked food (ater-ater) are sent from the priest’s house to village officials, and small earth offerings are set out by the roadside, cemetery, bridge, and other locations around the village (Hefner, 1985: 114). 

Manusia harus mengadakan pujan pada bulan purnama, tilem, galungan, panawangan, kasada, dan kapitu. Jika pujan dilaksanakan, Durga-Kala tidak akan mengganggu manusia. Ketiga Dewa tersebut terus-menerus mengajari manusia cara memuja dan memberikan sesaji kepada Durga-Kala sebagai manifestasi Sang Hyang Widhi (Sukmawan, 2018:123).
Examples:
Community members prepare shared food for the pujan ritual.
Pujan is led by a traditional ritual specialist (dukun adat).
Reference: Hefner, R. W. Hindu Javanese: Tengger Tradition and Islam.

Definition: A symbolic representation of the groom used in Tengger engagement riddles. Appearing in cangkriman customary riddles, it symbolizes the groom in the dialogue between families when exchanging rambon for djawi (representing the bride), reflecting the agrarian wisdom and linguistic artistry of the community.
Etymology:
rambon (rambOn) : I kn (sapi [x]) sapi turunane banthèng karo sapi lumrah. II kn: wangèn, ar. têmbako sing alus lan sêdhêp.
Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: In the engagement riddle tradition of the Tengger community, the groom's family symbolically refers to the prospective groom as rambon.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A traditional fermented drink made from glutinous rice and shrimp paste used in Tengger rituals. Served as a symbolic punishment during the cangkriman riddle game, it provokes spontaneous laughter to lighten the atmosphere while serving as a mild atonement in the sacred rite.
Etymology:
sajêng (saj|G) : K.N. een soort van sterken drank, arak.
Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16. sajěng : (sajöng) an alcoholic drink; palm wine; asajěngan palm wine maker; kasajěngan drunken.
Kawi Lexicon, Wojowasito, 1980, #575. sajeng : (sajöng) minuman keras; tuak; asajěngan pembuat tuak; kasajěngan mabuk.
Kawi - Indonesia, Wojowasito, 1977, #1019.
Examples: Participants who fail to answer a riddle in the cangkriman tradition drink sajeng as a symbolic punishment to lighten the atmosphere.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A traditional pregnancy ritual performed in Tengger before childbirth to pray for safety and a smooth delivery. In this ritual, a traditional midwife (dukun alit) prepares offerings on a woven tray (tampah), which are presented by her husband to Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa, with variations across different villages.
Etymology: "Makna dari upacara sesayut/sayut adalah agar bayi lahir dengan selamat dan lancar.  Pelaksanaan upacara sayud dilaksanakan berbeda-beda. Setiap desa di Tengger memiliki cara tersendiri untuk menggelarnya. Dalam ritual ini, dukun alit membuat sesaji yang lengkap dalam satu tampah. Sesaji tersebut diberikan kepada suami Bu Dukun untuk selanjutnya dihaturkan kepada Sang Hyang Widhi." (Sukmawan, 2020:103).
Examples: The Tengger community holds the Sayut ceremony before childbirth to pray for a safe and smooth delivery.
Reference:
- Sukmawan, Sony and Rahmi Febriani. 2018. “Perempuan-Perempuan Pemeluk Erat Adat: Studi Etnografi Perempuan Tengger.” Jurnal Linguista 2(1):1–10. Retrieved June 20, 2020 (http://e-journal.unipma.ac.id/index.php/ linguista/article/view/2682).
- Sukmawan, Sony and Rahmi Febriani. 2019. “Folklor Tengger: Literasi Harmoni Budaya, Instrumen Pendidikan, Konservasi, Dan Kewirausahaan.” Retrieved June 02, 2020 (https://www. researchgate.net/publication /332806987_Folklor_Tengger_Literasi_Harmoni_Budaya_Instrumen_Pendidikan_Konservasi_dan_Kewirausahaan).

Definition: A traditional wooden or bamboo tower used in Tengger for drying and storing post-harvest corn. The structure features a small roof at the top where tied corn is hung to dry in the mountain breeze, symbolizing local food security and ecological harmony.
Etymology: Sigirran adalah menara kayu atau bambu tempat menyimpan jagung yang telah dipanen, biasanya berbentuk tinggi dan ramping dengan atap kecil di puncaknya. Jagung digantung dalam ikatan dan dibiarkan kering secara alami oleh angin pegunungan (Jasper, 1928: 63). "Salah satu contoh sistem ketahanan pangan yang digunakan oleh masyarakat Tengger adalah sistem sigiran. Jagung-jagung yang telah dipanen tersebut dikeringkan di sigiran hingga jagung tersebut benar-benar kering dan dapat diolah menjadi makanan. Ketika jagung sudah kering, maka jagung akan awet dalam jangka waktu yang lama." (Sukmawan, 2022:132).
Examples: Tengger farmers hang their harvested corn on the sigirran to let it dry naturally in the mountain breeze.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S. dkk. (2022). Mendaras Puja, Mengemas Tamasya: Potensi Gastro- Sastra Wisata. Malang: MNC Publishing.

Definition: A ritual dance performed during the Karo celebration using sodor or kecrek. It symbolizes the struggle between two equal forces represented in crossed or face-to-face formations by four to six male or female dancers.
Etymology:
sodor (sOdOr) : K.N. een lans zonder scherpe punt, die bij de tournooispelen gebruikt wordt. -nyodor, met zulk een lans steken. -sodoran, met lansen zonder scherpe punten elkander steken; tournooispel.
Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16. 
sodor : KN. tournooilans, lans met een kwast aan de punt in plaats van ijzer (ook wel bij krijgsdansen gebruikt Wk., vrg. watang, jêgul, jêbêng). — nyodor, met een sòdòr steken of nazetten; ook met een lange stok of bamboe steken R. — nyodorake, een sodor, tot steken bezigen; daarmee (naar iem.) werpen Wk. — sodoran, elkander met sòdòr's steken; ook naam van een struikgewas met trosvruchten, waarvan de pitjes tot meel gemaakt worden, dat gebakken of gekookt gegeten wordt JR. — pasodoran, tournooiveld R.
Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: Dancers shake the bamboo sticks to produce rhythmic sounds while performing the Sodoran dance.

Definition: An offering container made of banana leaves shaped like a small box with pinched sides, used in rituals to hold offerings. Consisting of elements such as areca nuts, flowers, and cakes, its variant known as Takir Kurung also refers to a structural component of a traditional Javanese joglo house.
Etymology: takir (takIr) : kn. 1 wadhah panganan lsp. sing digawe godhong gêdhang dikuwungake dibitingi kiwa têngên; 2. ar. peranganing omah joglo awujud kayu katumpukan (sungsun) tumumpang ing pangêrêt lan panglari (sing manjêro); [x] ponthang: takir sing digawe janur ut. sing didèkèki janur ing kiwa têngên; di-[x]: digawe takir. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: Villagers prepare offerings placed in a banana-leaf takir to be presented during the Karo ceremony.
Reference:
- Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: A round flat tray made of woven bamboo strips, used for winnowing rice, drying food, and arranging ritual offerings in Javanese and Tengger traditions. Its circular form symbolizes wholeness and the interconnectedness of humans, nature, and the universe, representing receptivity to blessings in customary ceremonies.
Etymology: tampah : KN. (tèmpèh, OJ. Wk.) een van bamboe gevlochten wan of groot rond bord met opstaanden rand (wêngku, BTDj. 447) om rijst te wannen Wk., of ook om er iets op te droogen of uit te stallen (vgl. intêr, tapi, III, en tedhok). Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: The Tenggerese villagers arrange various offerings on a woven bamboo tampah during traditional ceremonies.
Reference: - Jasper, J. E. (1928). Tengger en de Tenggereezen. G. Kolff & Co.

Definition: A ritual leaf used in Tengger for animal sacrifice processions and ancestral effigies. Derived from the expression telu tok (only three), it symbolizes the Trimurti and the human life cycle of birth, life, and death, while its strong and flexible nature makes it ideal for binding symbolic structures.
Etymology: Dalam pelaksanaan mbeduduk, daun yang digunakan untuk mengikat hewan yang akan disembelih adalah daun tlotok. Tlotok memiliki arti telu tok (hanya tiga). Daun tersebut merupakan simbol dari ajaran agama Hindu yaitu Trimurti. Trimurti sendiri merupakan pedoman hidup umat Hindu yang berisi anjuran untuk berpikir yang baik, berbicara yang baik, dan berbuat yang baik. Selain makna simbolis, penggunaan daun tlotok dirasakan lebih mudah, lentur, dan bertekstur kuat jika dibandingkan dengan daun yang lainnya. Semakin mengering, daun tlotok akan semakin kuat. Daun tlotok juga digunakan sebagai media pembuatan Petra. Petra merupakan simbol arwah leluhur. Petra bagian atas (kepala) terbuat dari daun tlotok yang memiliki makna telu tok, yakni lahir, urip, mati. "Bagian atas petra (kepala) terbuat dari daun tlotok yang memiliki makna telu tok (hanya tiga). Tlotok merujuk kepada siklus hidup manusia, yakni lahir, hidup di dunia, dan mati. Daun-daun ini disiapkan oleh Pak Sepuh (asisten dukun Tengger)." (Sukmawan, 2022: 20-21).
Examples: The Tengger community uses tlotok leaves to bind sacrificial animals and construct the head structure of petra in customary rituals.
Reference: - Sukmawan, S., Firdaus, E. N., Salamah, & Ramadhani, A. K. (2022). Mendaras Puja, Mengemas Tamasya. Universitas Brawijaya Press (UB Press).

Definition: A traditional haircut ritual performed to mark a child’s transition from infancy to childhood. The ceremony involves trimming the tip of the child's hair (kuncung) accompanied by prayers and offerings as a plea for safety and healthy growth.
Etymology: tugêl (tug|l) : kn. 1 putung (marga dikêthok, dicoklèk lsp); 2 pêdhot tmr. dalan lsp. (marga katrajang liyane); 3 dipindhoni diluku malang; 4 paro, têngah, up. karo [x] = 1½, têlu [x] = 2½; di-[x]. diputung, dikêthok, dipêdhot; [x]-an. 1 olèh-olèhane nugêl, apa-apa sing wis tugêl; 2 paron, têngahan; 3 ks. maru. Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75. kuncung (kuncUG) : kn. 1 rambut (saèm. jambul) ing dhuwur bathuk; 2 ak. isih nganggo kuncung (tmr. bocah cilik); 3 pojoking ikêt kang nyongat ing sadhuwuring bathuk; 4 omah cilik sangarêping pêndhapa; wiwit [x] nganti gêlung pc: wiwit cilik nganti gêdhe; ngunjung, [x]-an: nganggo kuncung; di-[x]-i: 1 didokoki kuncung; Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75. gombak [Ind] : gombak, jambul, kuncung.Bausastra Indonesia-Jawi, Purwadarminta, c. 1939, #1979.
Examples: The Tengger community performs the tugel kuncung ritual when a child reaches four years of age as a symbol of safety and transition into childhood.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Proyek Sasana Budaya. (1978). Upacara Kasada dan beberapa adat istiadat masyarakat Tengger. Direktorat Jenderal Kebudayaan, Departemen Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.
- Sutarto, A. (2006). Sekilas tentang masyarakat Tengger. Balai Kajian Sejarah dan Nilai Tradisional Yogyakarta.

Definition: A symbolic title conferred upon the highest leader of the council of shamans in Tengger. The title is used during the cangkriman session of the Karo ritual to guide the sacred riddle dialogue, deliver judgments, and direct spiritual communication.
Etymology: tugur : KW. zva. tunggu, anggung, baris, Wk. KN. bij een werk, bij een feest, of op een post doorblijven, zonder naar huis te gaan RP. 9, JZ. I, 246, GR; werkelijk met die omschrijving Bl. CP. 246: tugur sadaya botên kalilan mantuk, volg. Wk. een buitengewone wacht doen, bv. bij de installatie, het huwelijk of overlijden van den Vorst; vgl. pakajangan, tunggu, poët. zva. baris, BS. bij Wk. KN. — nugur, hetz. — nuguri, ergens doorblijven op zijn post, onafgebroken bij of aan iets blijven; iemand onafgebroken blijven bewaken DW. 156, AS. 158, GR.; erg. of om iets een wacht als boven doen, bivouakeeren Wk.; ook zva. nunggoni, bv. nuguri umur, voor zijn leven zorgen. — nugurake, laten tugur, Waj. II, 94. — tuguran, mrv. v. tugur, Waj. II, 92; wachtdienst als boven; poët. (Wk. KN.) zva. barisan, KB. 84. — patuguran, poët. zva. pabarisan, KB. 84, Waj. II, 317.

Definition: A scared quinquennial ritual performed in Tengger during a leap month based on the synchronization of the lunar and solar calendars. The ceremony is held at the village's sacred site with a buffalo offering as a symbolic vehicle to the afterlife to cleanse the village from spirit disturbances and purify souls. Etymologically, it comes from the word tuna ("loss"), functioning to complete spiritual and moral shortcomings within an eight-year cycle.
Etymology:
Secara harfiah berarti ritual “to fill in” unan-unan diadakan setiap lima tahun sekali pada bulan kabisat yang terjadi karena adanya perbedaan antara kalender lunar dan kalender matahari yang digunakan oleh para pendeta Tengger. Diadakan di tempat suci desa, ritual ini membutuhkan persembahan seekor kerbau, yang dimaksudkan sebagai kendaraan menuju surga (Hefner, 1985, 123). 
Upacara ini dimaksudkan untuk membersihkan desa dari gangguan makhluk halus dan menyucikan para arwah yang belum sempurna agar dapat kembali ke alam asal yang sempurna, yaitu Nirwana. Kata unan-unan berasal dari kata tuna ‘rugi’, maksudnya upacara ini dapat melengkapi kekurangan-kekurangan yang diperbuat selama satu windu (Sutarto, 2006: 8). 
Setahun sekali diadakan festival besar Oenan-Oenan demi kebaikan desa, untuk setiap kesempatan biasanya seekor sapi atau kerbau disembelih (Jasper, 1927:23). "Unan-unan merupakan upacara adat masyarakat Tengger yang diseleggarakan setiap lima tahun sekali. Upacara ini bertujuan untuk membersihkan desa dan arwaharwah yang belum seutuhnya kembali ke tempat yang seharusnya. Selain itu, upacara ini bertujuan untuk melengkapi kekurangankekurangan yang belum dipenuhi dalam kurun waktu lima tahun berlalu." (Sukmawan, 2020:20)
Examples: The community sacrificed a buffalo as the main offering during the unan-unan ritual to purify the village and the souls of ancestors.
Reference:

Definition: A sacred wedding ritual performed in Tengger to ask for blessings from ancestors and the community for newlyweds. The procession serves as a request for permission to hold a celebration and functions as a fertility ritual to preserve local soil and water balance. During the ceremony, a traditional ritual specialist leads the marriage vows and prepares blessed water using young coconut or banana leaves as a sacred stirrer for safety prayers.
Examples: The Tengger community holds the walagara ceremony to request permission from ancestors and bless the newlyweds.
Reference:

Definition: An agrarian ethnic group inhabiting the Tengger highlands is East Java. They are known as strong preservers of ancestral traditions whose lives are closely tied to highland agricultural systems and Javanese-Hindu spiritual practices. Etymologically, the term refers to "people of the highlands" and now denotes the cultural and geographical identity of the Tengger community as a whole.
Etymology: wong (wOG) : orang, uwwèng, uwèng, nar, nra, nara, tiang, tiyang K., sujanma, sujalma, wwang, wwanga, wyajana, wyang, wyanga, wang, wong, wonga, wongha, wanggana, jana, janma, jalma, yana, manusa, manuswa, manusya, manuwya, manuja, manungsa, zie lanang en wadon; [pawongan]: kakawan, waracèthi, patiyangan, pagundhikan; Bausastra: Jarwa Kawi, Padmasusastra, 1903, #11. tênggêr : KN. hoog van een grooter of kleiner uitgestrektheid grond in vergelijking van den grond er naast of omheen (vrg. mênggêr). tênggêr-tênggêr, zva. punthuk-punthuk. gunung Tênggêr, het Těnggěr-gebergte. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.
Examples: Wong Tengger are known as an agrarian community who strongly preserve ancestral traditions and environmental balance around the Mount Bromo region.
Reference:
- Hefner, R. W. (1985). Hindu Javanese: Tengger tradition and Islam. Princeton University Press.
- Sukmawan, S., Rizal, M. S., & Nurmansyah, M. A. (2018). Green folklore. UB Press.

Definition: An ancient kingdom in folklore. Bantarangin refers to the Bantarangin Kingdom, which appears in the folklore associated with Reog Ponorogo. The kingdom was ruled by Prabu Klanasewandana and his prime minister, Bujangganong, who sought to propose to the princess of Kediri, Dewi Songgolangit, under conditions that ultimately led to the creation of the Reog performance tradition. Bantarangin is often portrayed as a prosperous and powerful kingdom, and its story serves as a narrative foundation for explaining the origins of Reog Ponorogo.
Examples: Archaeological findings in Dusun Seboto, such as large ancient bricks distributed across several sites, support historical explorations regarding the territory and existence of Bantarangin.
Categories: Social Structure, Space & Architecture, Local Knowledge

Definition: Brangkangan is a movement or posture resembling a tiger’s crawl, accompanied by head turns or swipes to the right and left, symbolizing vigilance and readiness in the tradition of performing arts.
Etymology:
tagahan; [ambrangkang]: rumangkang.
Bausastra: Jarwa Kawi, Padmasusastra, 1903, #11.
Examples: The Reog dancer performs the brangkangan movement deftly while turning their head to the right and left to depict the vigilance of a tiger.

Definition: A cantrik is a student or disciple who studies under the guidance of a spiritual figure or the leader of a spiritual retreat (such as a warok in the Reog tradition), faithfully following him wherever he goes to gain knowledge and learn the rituals and traditions of that way of life.
Etymology:
kn. abdining pandhita ngiras dadi murid; nyantrik: ngabdi marang pandhita.
Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: A cantrik faithfully serves and follows the warok wherever he goes to learn the knowledge and traditions of the padepokan.

Definition: A tiger-like mask representing the Lodaya Kingdom. Dadak Merak, also known as Singobarong, represents King Singabarong of the Lodaya Kingdom and unites two contrasting symbols in a single form: the strength and authority of the tiger, regarded as the ruler of the jungle, and the elegance and allure of the peacock. Physically, Dadak Merak takes the shape of a tiger head mask with an open mouth, carved from lightweight wood (such as randoe or dadap), covered with tiger skin and fitted with a beard, while a whole preserved peacock is attached at the neck with its tail arranged artistically to fan out, reaching a height of around one and a half meters.
Etymology:
dhadhak : KW. zva. bêbuka, Wk.; volg. Wk. Definition: A woven bamboo horse prop. Eblek is a woven bamboo horse decorated to resemble a war horse, used as a prop by the Jathil dancer to depict a horseman on the battlefield through agile and dynamic movements. Eblek symbolizes the control of human desire, as horses known for their strong impulses are guided with reins or blinders, just as humans must learn to restrain their own desires and lust, which is the greatest battle of the human beings.
Etymology:

Ook èblèk, of èblèkan, een los vloertje van gevlochten bamboe, bv. in een muizenval, daar het lokaas op gelegd wordt J. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.

Examples: As a cultural artifact, Eblek symbolizes the control of human desire, reflecting how horses with strong impulses are guided with reins or blinders.

Definition: A hip-swaying movement in dances. Edrek is a hip-swaying movement in the Jathil Reog Obyog dance, performed as a playful signal or tease directed toward the Singa Barong, Pujangganong, and the audience. The dancer approaches the pembarong or Pujangganong and concludes the movement by shaking the hips or buttocks toward their face, which is traditionally believed to provide an energetic “boost” or encouragement to the performer.
Etymology:
goyang (goyaG) : K.N. schudden, heên en weêr bewegen, roeren, in beweging brengen, luiden [Sd.Ml.id.]. goyang kapala, het hoofd schudden.
Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16.
Examples: During the performance, the dancer approaches the pembarong or Pujangganong and concludes the movement by shaking the hips or buttocks toward their face.

Definition: A young male dancer in performances. Gemblak refers to a young male dancer who traditionally accompanied a warok in Reog Ponorogo performances, taking the role of the jathil, a horse-riding warrior, and wearing feminine-style attire such as a skirt, chest covering, and earrings as part of the symbolic presentation. The relationship between warok and gemblak was understood as a father–child spiritual bond, in which the warok practiced strict ascetic discipline, including abstaining from sexual relations, and the gemblak assisted the warok in daily needs as an expression of devotion rather than sexual orientation. Starting in the 1980s, the role of gemblak as jathil dancer was gradually replaced by women, marking a significant change in the Reog Ponorogo tradition.
Etymology:
gêmblak (g|mbla?) : I êngg. kn:gêndul cilik. II kn: tukang gawe dandanan kuningan. III (ut. [x]-an) kn: lèdhèk lanang; ng-[x]: ndhêmêni padha lanang. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.

gêmblak : geelkoperwerker WG. 200; dial. = gêndul cilik, de N. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederlandsch Handwoordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1901, #918.

Examples: The relationship between warok and gemblak was understood as a spiritual bond rooted in spiritual needs, where the warok practiced ascetic discipline while the gemblak assisted in daily needs as an expression of devotion.

Definition: A tassel made of strands of thread or cord used as an ornament on traditional clothing or cultural artifacts. Used in performing arts costumes such as Reog, these yellow and red tassels are attached to pants or dance costumes to enhance the dancers’ appearance.
Etymology:
gombyok (gOmbyO?) : kn. 1 bolah sutra lsp. sing digawe rompyo-rompyo kanggo rêrênggan; 2 oncèn kêmbang ing kêris; di-[x]-i. dirêngga nganggo gombyok.
Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: The Reog dancer's costume is adorned with yellow and red gombyok on the pants to enhance the beauty of the movements while dancing.

Definition: A cavalry dance depicting a knightly figure. Jathil is a cavalry dance depicting a knightly figure with patriotic spirit and unwavering devotion to the nation, expressed through its narrative and dynamic, energetic movements, traditionally performed by male dancers (talèdèk lanang). Broadly, the Jathil dance has two main versions based on different understandings of Reog’s origins: the Bantarangin version, which is commonly presented in formal festival performances, and the Ki Ageng Kutu or Wengker version, known as Jathil Reog Obyog. Both versions convey themes of heroism and steadfast loyalty within the Reog Ponorogo artistic tradition.
Etymology:
jathil (jaTIl) : jathilan Ngt., Sm. (M.) reyok, tlèdhèk lanang. Sumber: Javaansche Woordenlijst, De Nooy, 1893, #24.

jathil (jaTIl) : n-[x] kn njogèd nunggang jaran kepang; [x]-an: ar. tontonan jêjogèdan nganggo nunggang jaran kepang. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.

jathil : [x]-an a dance performed while astraddle a woven-bamboo horse (jaran kepang) accompanied by angklung music. n-[x] to perform this dance. Sumber: Javanese-English Dictionary, Horne, 1974, #1968."
Examples: A group of jathil performers appears as part of a Reog performance.

Definition: A powerful king of the Bantarangin Kingdom. Klono Sewandono is the king of the Bantarangin Kingdom in the Reog tradition, portrayed as a handsome, brave, and powerful ruler. In his dance performance, he wields the Samandiman whip, which has five strands (jabung sayet), symbolizing the strength of faith. This represents the belief that a true leader must possess firm faith grounded in the five pillars of Islam: the shahada, prayer, fasting, zakat, and hajj.
Examples: In his dance performance, Klanasewandana wields the Samandiman whip, which has five strands (jabung sayet) symbolizing the strength of faith.

Definition: Kolor refers to loose black pants that are part of the warok costume. The material used is typically strong and comfortable, such as Nagata Drill fabric. These pants are worn by the warok to create a majestic and powerful appearance during performances.

A tradition of visiting and cleaning the graves of ancestors, held during the month of Sha’ban as a form of respect and prayer for the well-being of the spirits of the departed. Practiced in Javanese culture, this ritual involves cleaning the grave site, offering collective prayers to God, and scattering flowers as a gesture of devotion from descendants to their ancestors.
Etymology: nyadran (¥adran) : kn. slamêtan (sêsaji) ing papan kang kramat; kc. sadran. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: The villagers gather at the cemetery to perform the nyadran tradition by cleaning ancestor graves and offering collective prayers ahead of the month of Ramadan.

Definition: Nyantrik is a tradition or practice in which one becomes a disciple and serves a spiritual teacher or the leader of a spiritual retreat (such as a warok), by faithfully following them to gain spiritual knowledge, martial arts skills, and cultural insights.
Etymology: dadi murid: ngabdi marang pandhita Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.
Examples: The young initiate undergoes the nyantrik practice by serving the warok to absorb spiritual wisdom and the cultural ethics of Reog performance.

Definition: A legendary whip associated with kings. Pecut Samandiman is the legendary whip associated with King Klanasewandana in the Reog Ponorogo tradition, and it also refers to a popular whip performance art found in Kediri and surrounding regions. As a cultural artifact, Pecut Samandiman is believed to hold supernatural power. As a performance practice, it appears in festivals, competitions, and staged presentations that blend choreography and rhythmic movement, and it can even be used to pull vehicles or create loud sounds.
Etymology:
pêcut (p|cUt) : kn. cêmêthi garane dawa di-[x](-i): 1 disabêt(-i) ing pêcut 2 pc. digirèkake supaya mêmpêng. Sumber: Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.

pêcut (p|cUt) : K.N. een lange zweep [Sd. zweep. Vrg. cêmêthi en têmbung]. -mêcut, met een lange zweep slaan, zweepen. Sumber: Javaansch-Nederduitsch Woordenboek, Gericke en Roorda, 1847, #16.

Examples: As a cultural artifact, Pecut Samandiman is believed to hold supernatural power and is used as an ultimate weapon to overcome falsehood and evil.

Definition: A warlord figure from the Bantarangin Kingdom. Pujangga Anom, also known as Pujangganong or Bujanganom, is a warlord figure from the Bantarangin Kingdom who embodies an energetic, agile, and acrobatic military leader, reflecting the noble qualities of a patih who is devoted and responsible in managing the kingdom's strategic affairs. His lively and acrobatic dance movements make this character especially appealing to audiences, accompanied by the use of a mask with bulging eyes as a symbol of sharpness, alertness, and precision in carrying out the commands of King Prabu Klono Sewandono. Physically, the dancer typically wears a white half-face mask with a blunt nose, identified as the Pëntoel mask, although according to Mr. Staugaard, there are also dancers who use black masks referred to by the same name, indicating variations in how this figure is represented in Reog performances.
Etymology:
pujăngga : tiyang ingkang sampurna kawruhipun ing bab kasusastran. Pujăngga: puja + angga, puja: nênuwun ing Gusti Allah, angga: badan. Pujăngga yèn tiyang Walandi: Professor. Babasan lan Saloka, Anonim, 1908, #1278.

Examples: Also known as Pujangganong or Bujanganom, Pujangga Anom is a warlord figure from the Bantarangin Kingdom who embodies an energetic, agile, and acrobatic military leader.

Definition: An early form of Reog from Bantarangin. Reog Bantarangin is considered the earliest form of Reog, originating from the Bantarangin Kingdom (the western river bank version). It features a complex dance-drama structure with characters such as the Warok that is the horse-riding Jathil warriors, Patih Bujangganing, Prabu Klomosewandana, and Dadak Merak. This version presents the storyline with clearly defined roles for each character and follows a strict, standardized performance structure.
Etymology:
Reog (Reog) : kn ar. tontonan bngs. jathilan (padha nunggang jaran kepang). Bausastra Jawa, Poerwadarminta, 1939, #75.

Definition: A participatory Wengker-style Reog Ponorogo performance. Reog Obyog is a participatory and entertaining form of the Wengker-style Reog Ponorogo, typically performed in open spaces such as village squares or home courtyards during celebrations or village cleansing rituals. It emphasizes togetherness between the dancers and the audience, without a rigid performance structure.
